Systemic racism and bias have led to entrenched racial disparities in both incarceration and economic well-being. In more than half of all counties in 2019, Black people were more than twice as likely as white people to be incarcerated in jail. In these high-disparity counties, Black households earned on average $22,552 less than white households and were more than twice as likely to be in poverty. sources.page_context: ich is the biggest measure of the vast reach of jails. Directly wrestling with the issue of race and incarceration remains uncomfortable ground because it forces people to confront a deep legacy of racism and its connection to our system of incarceration in this country, past and present. Key Facts Black people are still 3.6x more likely to be incarcerated in local jails nationally than white people. Between 2005 and 2013, the black jail incarceration rate declined by 20% nationally. Since 2005, black incarceration rates have dropped 30% in urban areas and 22% in suburban areas. Since 2008, black incarceration rates have dropped 14% in small/ medium metros and 2% in rural areas.
